text: McTaggart notes that every event must be past, present, and future -- an apparent contradiction. Why does relativizing these to different times (E is future at t1, present at t2, past at t3) fail to remove the contradiction?
choices: Because the B-series relations among t1, t2, and t3 are themselves constantly changing
Because presentism entails that t1 and t3 do not exist, leaving the relativization without a truthmaker
Because the times t1, t2, and t3 must each themselves be past, present, and future, so the same contradiction reappears one level up, generating a vicious regress
Because special relativity denies that there is any objective fact about which time is present
explanation: McTaggart grants the reply but observes that saying E is future/present/past AT t1, t2, t3 just re-describes those times with A-properties -- and each of t1, t2, t3 must in turn be past, present, and future, so the contradiction recurs endlessly. That is why the regress is vicious rather than harmless. Option 0 misdescribes B-relations (which are permanent), while options 1 and 3 substitute presentism and relativity for McTaggart's own reasoning.
